01

Introduction

An airfoil is the cross-sectional shape of a wing or aerodynamic surface designed to generate lift when air flows around it. Its geometry, typically a curved upper surface and a flatter or differently curved lower surface, changes how air moves around it and creates a pressure distribution that produces an aerodynamic force. The shape also determines lift, drag and stall behavior, which makes airfoil design essential in aircraft wings, propellers and turbines.

A compliant airfoil is one whose shape can change through the elastic deformation of its structure, rather than relying only on traditional hinges and movable control surfaces. Instead of rigid parts rotating relative to each other, compliant mechanisms let sections of the airfoil bend in a controlled way and modify its aerodynamic profile. This can give smoother transitions, fewer gaps and discontinuities in the surface, and potentially better aerodynamic efficiency with lower mechanical complexity and weight.

02

Motive

The Student Community Aeronautic Society of Tec de Monterrey (SAERO) has a section dedicated to research and development of aeronautics projects. In the August–December 2025 semester it set itself the goal of developing, building and flying a remote-controlled aircraft that used compliant airfoils.

My role was the design and prototyping of the compliant airfoil. The project eventually stagnated because of management problems and the approaching final exams, but I still made significant progress on the airfoil and on building it into a wing, which is what I present below.

03

Design

The design began by breaking an airfoil’s complex geometry into simpler shapes, assuming they were rigid linkages with freely rotating joints. An airfoil turned out to be essentially a half circle, a rectangle and a triangle. Slide the top and bottom linkages of the rectangle in opposite directions and the triangle, which represents the trailing edge, points up or down.

It was a good starting concept, but it needed changes before it could become a physical model. As a compliant mechanism, the airfoil can’t have rotary joints: every motion must come from bending, twisting or buckling the linkages. The many points of contact between the shapes would also demand a great deal of shear force to deform.

Because the leading edge is linked to the central rectangle, it also bends in the opposite direction to the trailing edge. That may help channel the airstream, but both edges remain attached to a central section that keeps its relative angle, so the airfoil contorts into a sideways S whenever it shears, which disrupts its aerodynamics.

The fix was to cut the airfoil where the top linkage of the rectangle meets the semicircle. The mechanism then bends with much less shear force and the leading edge stays at a fixed angle. The cut exposes the inside of the airfoil to the outside air, so a sleeve extends from the leading edge over the sliding section of the top surface without being attached to it, keeping the airfoil a single piece. The sleeve is not shown in the Video 2 demonstration, but it is present in the 3D model below.

Ignoring the linkages and rotating joints and returning to the compliant mechanism, the airfoil divides into three sections: a rigid section at the front, a bending section in the middle and a rigid section at the end. For visualization, the finalized linkage model includes an internal servomotor whose shaft arm connects to the upper edge of the central rectangle, providing the force that bends the whole airfoil.

Reducing the load on the servomotor stayed the main challenge throughout development, which is why several design modifications were tested on printed sections like this one.

04

Construction

Once the basics were settled, the dimensions were defined. The airfoil was going to be 3D printed, so every wall was given a thickness of 0.5 mm, the smallest consistent thickness our printer allowed. The airfoil also had to fit an internal 9 g servomotor and the rotating arm that produces the bending.

Wings of various lengths were printed and tested. Even with all the modifications above, the airfoil still needs significant force to bend, and a single servo could not bend the control surface of an entire wing. So the wing is divided into multiple identical segments, all connected by the wing spars, each with its own servomotor.

The mechanism isn’t exclusive to this airfoil: it can be applied to any NACA airfoil, as long as it is scaled to fit the internal servo and arm.

05

Conclusions

Even though the project it was made for never materialized, I’m satisfied with what I produced. Reducing the load on the servomotor remained the main challenge throughout development.

This is only one of many possible compliant wing and airfoil mechanisms, but I believe the simple, monolithic design will suit small, cheap and efficient UAVs. It is a stepping stone toward full compliant control surfaces in aviation, a change poised to bring better fuel economy to all sorts of aeronautic applications.
